\begin{document}

\title{Symmetry control of exceptional structure in the massive scalar
quasinormal spectrum of doubly rotating five-dimensional Myers--Perry black
holes}

\author{\TODO{author names not assigned}}
\affiliation{\TODO{affiliation not assigned}}

\date{\today}

\begin{abstract}
We ask how the enhanced equal-spin symmetry of the asymptotically flat, doubly
rotating five-dimensional Myers--Perry black hole organizes exceptional
(defective) structure in its massive scalar quasinormal spectrum. Two results
are structural and exact. First, because $\partial_\phi$ and $\partial_\psi$ are
Killing for arbitrary rotation parameters, the quasinormal pencil is a direct
sum over azimuthal sectors $(m_1,m_2)$, and the Jordan chains of a direct sum
are the union of the summands' chains; a coincidence of frequencies belonging to
different sectors is therefore always semisimple. This closes the equal-spin
$U(2)$ multiplet channel exactly: those degeneracies are protected from
splitting \emph{and} forbidden from becoming exceptional by one and the same
fact. Second, the residual discrete symmetry is a Klein four-group acting on
parameters \emph{and} sector labels, so diagonal sectors $m_1=m_2$ are exactly
even in the spin asymmetry $\delta=(a-b)/2$ while anti-diagonal sectors
$m_1=-m_2$ are exactly even in $s=(a+b)/2$; any exceptional line in a diagonal
sector must occur in mirror pairs and terminate quadratically on the equal-spin
surface rather than crossing it. We then search the one surviving channel ---
collisions between different $(\ell,N)$ branches within a fixed sector --- with
a branch atlas of $50\,558$ continued points across seven sectors, three angular
branches and four overtones each. Three rescaling-invariant diagnostics are
bounded away from zero: the pairwise branch gap by $0.5116$, a Cauchy
root-separation estimator by $0.3107$, and the local discriminant by $0.2618$,
with the eigenvalue condition number at the strongest interaction finite at
$8.73\times10^{3}$ against $18.3$ at an ordinary control mode. The ten tightest
candidates are classified as avoided crossings by argument-principle, monodromy
and Puiseux tests. We find no exceptional point in the searched domain and no
exceptional phenomenology in the corresponding ringdown: the strongest
interactions split in the damping rate rather than the oscillation frequency.
The result contrasts with the exceptional lines established for the de Sitter
members of this family, whose mechanism is tied to the near-Nariai structure and
has no $\Lambda=0$ analogue.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

%=========================================================================
\section{Introduction}\label{sec:intro}
%=========================================================================

Quasinormal modes are the resonances of a black hole, the poles of its
scattering Green function, and the observable content of the ringdown
\cite{Kokkotas1999D46,Berti2009D47,Konoplya2011D48,Bertietal2025D50}. Because
the underlying operator is not self-adjoint, they carry structure with no
Hermitian analogue. The most striking is the \emph{exceptional point} (EP): a
parameter value at which two or more eigenvalues \emph{and} their eigenvectors
coalesce, leaving the generator defective
\cite{KatoE71,Bergholtz2019E63,Ashida2020E64}. At an EP the resolvent acquires a
pole of order two, the mode expansion ceases to be a basis, and the time-domain
response develops a secular $t\,e^{-i\omega t}$ component
\cite{PanossoMacedoetal2025B30,Motohashi2024B24}.

Exceptional structure is by now well documented across black-hole spectroscopy.
Branching of quasinormal modes was identified for nearly extremal Kerr
\cite{Yangetal2012B18}; eigenvalue repulsions organize the Kerr--Newman
spectrum \cite{Diasetal2021B19,Dias2022B20,Davey2023B21}; genuine exceptional
points and hysteresis appear in massive-scalar Kerr
\cite{Cavalcante2024B22,Cavalcante2024B23,Cavalcante2025B29}; and resonant
excitation near such points has been analysed in detail
\cite{Oshita2025B25,Yang2025B26,Kubota2025B27,Caoetal2025B28}. Most directly
relevant here, continuous \emph{exceptional lines} have been established in
massive-scalar Kerr--de Sitter and Myers--Perry--de Sitter, where the near-Nariai
limit reduces the radial problem to a P\"oschl--Teller form and permits a
semi-analytic treatment \cite{Nakamoto2026A17,Daveyetal2022A13}. The
non-Hermitian literature supplies the organizing framework: exceptional sets are
generically of codimension two, and symmetry can both protect them and change
their codimension \cite{Bergholtz2019E63,Mandal2021E65,Zhangetal2022E66}.

The five-dimensional Myers--Perry black hole \cite{Myers1986A01,Emparan2008A02}
is an unusually favourable arena for asking whether that machinery has a
gravitational realization with \emph{two} rotation parameters. The massive
Klein--Gordon equation separates \cite{Murata2007A03,Wu2008A04}, the massive
scalar spectrum with two arbitrary spins has been computed
\cite{Huang2025A16,Lietal2023A15,Lu2023A14}, and --- crucially --- the isometry
group is enhanced at equal angular momenta,
$\mathbb{R}\times U(1)\times U(1)\to\mathbb{R}\times SU(2)\times U(1)$, rendering
the metric cohomogeneity-one \cite{Murata2008A06}. That enhancement produces
exact degeneracies. The natural expectation, and the standard mechanism for
symmetry-protected exceptional structure in non-Hermitian systems
\cite{Zhangetal2022E66,Mandal2021E65}, is that breaking the symmetry should
unfold those degeneracies into exceptional points.

\emph{We show that this expectation fails, and fails for an exact reason.} Both
azimuthal Killing vectors survive for arbitrary rotation parameters, so the
quasinormal pencil decomposes as a direct sum over azimuthal sectors. The Jordan
chains of a direct sum are the union of the summands' chains; consequently a
coincidence of frequencies from different sectors is always semisimple. The
equal-spin multiplet degeneracies are protected from splitting \emph{and}
forbidden from becoming defective by one and the same fact. This is not a
statement about how hard one looks --- it holds at every point of parameter
space.

The closure redirects the question rather than ending it, and the paper follows
the redirection. We classify the residual discrete symmetry, derive what it
would impose on an exceptional line if one existed, and then search the single
channel the no-go leaves open, with methods calibrated so that a negative result
is meaningful.

Section~\ref{sec:setup} fixes conventions. Section~\ref{sec:nogo} proves the
decomposition and the no-go. Section~\ref{sec:group} classifies the symmetry
group and derives a termination law. Section~\ref{sec:methods} describes the
solvers and the diagnostics --- including why the derivative of a spectral
condition cannot bound anything, and what replaces it.
Sections~\ref{sec:atlas} and~\ref{sec:result} present the atlas and the
exclusion. Section~\ref{sec:consequences} covers the effective model,
pseudospectra and ringdown. Section~\ref{sec:quasiresonant} resolves a
solver-domain question that turns out to be physics.
Section~\ref{sec:limits} states the limitations without softening them.

%=========================================================================
\section{Setup and conventions}\label{sec:setup}
%=========================================================================

The five-dimensional Myers--Perry metric with two rotation parameters $a,b$
\cite{Myers1986A01} in Boyer--Lindquist-like coordinates $(t,r,\theta,\phi,\psi)$
with $\theta\in[0,\pi/2]$ reads
\begin{align}
  ds^2 =& -dt^2 + \frac{M}{\Sigma}\big(dt - a\sin^2\!\theta\,d\phi
        - b\cos^2\!\theta\,d\psi\big)^2 \nonumber\\
       &+ \frac{\Sigma}{\Delta}dr^2 + \Sigma\,d\theta^2 \nonumber\\
       &+ (r^2+a^2)\sin^2\!\theta\,d\phi^2 + (r^2+b^2)\cos^2\!\theta\,d\psi^2,
\end{align}
with $\Sigma = r^2 + a^2\cos^2\!\theta + b^2\sin^2\!\theta$,
$\Pi=(r^2+a^2)(r^2+b^2)$ and $\Delta = (\Pi - Mr^2)/r^2$. Here $M$ is the mass
parameter (dimension length$^2$), \emph{not} the scalar mass, which we write
$\mu$. We use $\Phi\sim e^{-i\omega t}$, so damped modes have $\Imm\,\omega<0$,
and set $M=1$.

Throughout we use the adapted rotation coordinates
\begin{equation}
  s=\frac{a+b}{2},\qquad \delta=\frac{a-b}{2},
\end{equation}
so $\delta=0$ is the equal-spin surface. Horizon radii satisfy $z_\pm=r_\pm^2$
with $z_+z_-=a^2b^2$; we quote the inner horizon as $r_-$, noting that
$z_-=r_-^2$ --- a distinction that has caused confusion in this literature and
which we flag because a domain guard written in one variable is quantitatively
different in the other.

The massive Klein--Gordon equation separates
\cite{Murata2007A03,Wu2008A04,Frolovetal2018A09}. We re-derived the separation
symbolically from the metric in exact rational arithmetic rather than
transcribing it, and every convention below is re-derived by an automated test
on each run. Two exact consequences are used repeatedly. The angular problem is
spheroidal \cite{Berti2005A05}, with spheroidicity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:c2}
  c^2 = (\omega^2-\mu^2)(a^2-b^2) = 4\,s\,\delta\,(\omega^2-\mu^2),
\end{equation}
which vanishes identically on $\delta=0$ \emph{and} on $s=0$; on both surfaces
the angular operator is the round Laplacian on $S^3$, with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Lambda}
  \Lambda\big|_{\delta=0} = \ell(\ell+2),
  \qquad \ell = 2n+|m_1|+|m_2|,\quad n\ge0 .
\end{equation}
Moreover, at $\delta=0$ the radial equation and the horizon condition depend on
$(m_1,m_2)$ only through $m=m_1+m_2$. The quasinormal boundary conditions are
ingoing at the horizon and outgoing at infinity, with exponents
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bcs}
  (z-z_+)^{-i\sigma_+},\quad
  \sigma_+=\frac{\omega-m_1\Omega_a-m_2\Omega_b}{2\kappa},
  \qquad e^{i\Omega r}r^{-3/2},
\end{equation}
where $\Omega=\sqrt{\omega^2-\mu^2}$. Because $D-3=2$ the radial potential is
exactly even in $r$ and carries no $1/r$ tail: unlike four-dimensional massive
Kerr \cite{DetweilerD53,Dolan2007D55} there is no Coulomb phase, and the
asymptotic exponent is exactly $-3/2$. Figure~\ref{fig:spectrum} shows the
resulting spectrum and the region of it covered by this work.

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig1_spectrum.pdf}
  \caption{The spectrum and the atlas coverage. (a) All $50\,558$ continued
  points of sector $(1,1)$ in the complex frequency plane, coloured by overtone
  $N$ and marked by angular branch $\ell$. The branches form well-separated
  clusters throughout the searched domain; the exclusion of
  Sec.~\ref{sec:result} is the quantitative version of that separation.
  (b) The same branches followed under the scalar mass $\mu$ at fixed background
  $s=0.20$, $\delta=0$: increasing $\mu$ moves each mode to larger
  $\Rem\,\omega$ and smaller damping.}
  \label{fig:spectrum}
\end{figure*}

%=========================================================================
\section{Sector decomposition and the cross-sector no-go}\label{sec:nogo}
%=========================================================================

\subsection{The decomposition}

No metric component depends on $\phi$ or $\psi$, so $\partial_\phi$ and
$\partial_\psi$ are Killing for \emph{arbitrary} $a,b$ --- not only on the
equal-spin surface. The torus $T^2=S^1_\phi\times S^1_\psi$ therefore acts on
the space carrying the quasinormal pencil by
\begin{equation}
  (R_{\alpha\beta}u)(t,r,\theta,\phi,\psi)=u(t,r,\theta,\phi-\alpha,\psi-\beta).
\end{equation}

A natural objection is that quasinormal eigenfunctions are not $L^2$ --- they
diverge at infinity --- so a Fourier decomposition justified in $L^2(T^2)$ need
not apply. The objection is answered by not using $L^2$ at all. Let $X$ be any
Banach space on which the pencil $T(\omega)$ is defined: weighted,
hyperboloidal, or analytic with prescribed boundary behaviour; the choice is
immaterial for what follows. The action $R_{\alpha\beta}$ is by bounded
invertible operators and is strongly continuous, because it relabels two compact
coordinates and touches neither $r$ nor the boundary conditions
\eqref{eq:bcs} that define $X$. For a compact abelian group acting strongly
continuously by bounded operators on a Banach space, the isotypic projections
\begin{equation}
  \Pi_{m_1m_2}=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^2}\iint e^{-i(m_1\alpha+m_2\beta)}
  R_{\alpha\beta}\,d\alpha\,d\beta
\end{equation}
are bounded, mutually orthogonal idempotents summing strongly to the identity.
This is Fourier analysis for compact group representations and requires no inner
product. The horizon exponent in \eqref{eq:bcs} depends only on the sector's own
labels and the condition at infinity does not involve them, so the domain is
itself a direct sum and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:directsum}
  T(\omega)=\bigoplus_{(m_1,m_2)\in\mathbb{Z}^2}T_{m_1m_2}(\omega).
\end{equation}
The compact directions carry the argument; the radial functional setting never
enters. We stress that \eqref{eq:directsum} is a decomposition over
$(m_1,m_2)$ \emph{only}, and does not use separation of variables in $\theta$ ---
a point that matters in Sec.~\ref{sec:nogo:closes}.

\subsection{The no-go}

\begin{lemma}[Jordan structure of a direct sum]\label{lem:directsum}
Let $T(\omega)=\bigoplus_k T_k(\omega)$ on a direct-sum domain. The generalized
eigenvectors of $T$ at $\omega_*$ are exactly the direct sums of generalized
eigenvectors of the summands, and the maximal Jordan-chain length of $T$ at
$\omega_*$ equals the maximum over $k$ of that of $T_k$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
A chain $v_0,\dots,v_{q-1}$ satisfies
$\sum_{i} T^{(i)}(\omega_*)v_{j-i}/i!=0$ for each $j$. Applying the bounded
commuting projector $\Pi_k$ to each equation shows the components $\Pi_k v_j$
form a chain in block $k$; conversely a chain in one block extends by zero.
Hence the chains of $T$ are superpositions of chains of the $T_k$, and the
longest chain of $T$ is the longest occurring in a single block.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:nogo}
A coincidence of quasinormal frequencies belonging to \emph{distinct} azimuthal
sectors cannot be defective. The total pencil is defective at $\omega_*$ if and
only if some single sector is already defective there.
\end{corollary}

Corollary~\ref{cor:nogo} carries no hypothesis on the multiplicity within each
block, which is why it is stated at the level of Jordan structure rather than as
a statement about simple eigenvalues. The underlying algebra is standard
\cite{KatoE71}; what is specific to this system is that the decomposition
\eqref{eq:directsum} holds for \emph{all} $a,b$, so the conclusion is not
confined to the symmetric surface.

\subsection{What this closes}\label{sec:nogo:closes}

By \eqref{eq:Lambda} and the $m$-dependence at $\delta=0$, the degenerate set at
fixed $(\ell,m)$ consists of all $(m_1,m_2)$ with $m_1+m_2=m$,
$|m_1|+|m_2|\le\ell$ and $\ell-|m_1|-|m_2|$ even. For $m\ge0$ the value
$|m_1|+|m_2|=m$ is attained by the $m+1$ pairs with $m_2\in[0,m]$, and each
value $m+2j$ with $j\ge1$ by exactly two pairs; the constraint admits
$j\le(\ell-m)/2$, so the multiplet dimension is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:multiplet}
  (m+1)+2\cdot\tfrac{\ell-m}{2}=\ell+1,
\end{equation}
\emph{independently of $m$}. The case $m<0$ follows by the parity generator of
Sec.~\ref{sec:group}. With $\ell+1$ allowed values of $m$ the level total is
$(\ell+1)^2$, the dimension of the $SO(4)$ scalar harmonic level, as it must be.
Figure~\ref{fig:multiplet}(c) verifies \eqref{eq:multiplet} exactly.

These are precisely the degeneracies the enhanced equal-spin symmetry produces.
Their members carry distinct $(m_1,m_2)$, hence occupy decoupled blocks, hence
--- by Corollary~\ref{cor:nogo} --- cannot be defective at any $\delta$. The
protection mechanism and the obstruction are the same fact.
Figure~\ref{fig:multiplet}(a) shows the degeneracy and its lifting: sectors
$(1,1)$ and $(2,0)$, which share $m=2$, meet exactly at $\delta=0$ and separate
for $\delta\ne0$.

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig2_multiplet.pdf}
  \caption{Equal-spin structure. (a) Sectors $(1,1)$ and $(2,0)$ share
  $m=m_1+m_2=2$ and are exactly degenerate at $\delta=0$
  ($\ell=2$, $N=0$, $s=0.20$, $\mu=0.6$); the degeneracy is semisimple by
  Corollary~\ref{cor:nogo}. (b) The $\delta$-parity of Sec.~\ref{sec:group},
  measured: the diagonal sector $(1,1)$ satisfies
  $\omega(+\delta)=\omega(-\delta)$ to machine precision, while the off-diagonal
  sector $(2,0)$ violates it by $\sim10^{-2}$ --- thirteen orders of magnitude
  of separation, and a negative control showing the evenness is a property of
  the sector rather than an artifact of a $\delta$-blind solver.
  (c) The multiplet dimension \eqref{eq:multiplet} is exactly $\ell+1$ for every
  allowed $m$, verified to $\ell=40$ (shown to $\ell=12$).}
  \label{fig:multiplet}
\end{figure*}

The search must therefore move \emph{inside} a fixed sector. There, different
$\ell$ are \emph{not} decoupled blocks: the angular eigenvalue $\Lambda_j(\omega)$
depends on $\omega$, so distinct $\ell$ are branches of one analytic family and
nothing forbids them from colliding defectively. This is exactly why
\eqref{eq:directsum} was set up without invoking separation of variables --- the
angular decomposition is a computational convenience within a sector, not a
block structure. The within-sector channel is the surviving target, and the rest
of the paper addresses it.

%=========================================================================
\section{The residual symmetry group and a termination law}\label{sec:group}
%=========================================================================

Two generators act on the pair (parameters, sector labels):
\begin{align}
  E:\ &(a,b,m_1,m_2)\mapsto(b,a,m_2,m_1), \\
  P:\ &(a,b,m_1,m_2)\mapsto(-a,-b,-m_1,-m_2).
\end{align}
$E$ relabels the two rotation planes; $P$ is the isometry $\phi\to-\phi$,
$\psi\to-\psi$ composed with reversing both rotation senses. Both are exact for
arbitrary $a,b,\mu$, and $\{1,E,P,EP\}\cong\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2$. In
adapted coordinates $E:(s,\delta)\to(s,-\delta)$, $P:(s,\delta)\to(-s,-\delta)$
and $EP:(s,\delta)\to(-s,\delta)$.

Crucially, \emph{no generator acts on the parameters alone} --- each also moves
the sector. A symmetry of the parameter space at fixed sector therefore exists
only in sectors stabilized by the corresponding element:

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
sector & stabilizer & consequence \\
\midrule
$m_1=m_2$ & $E$ & $\omega$ exactly even in $\delta$ \\
$m_1=-m_2$ & $EP$ & $\omega$ exactly even in $s$ \\
$(0,0)$ & all of $G$ & even in $\delta$ \emph{and} in $s$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Stabilizers and the parameter-space symmetries they induce. All three
are verified numerically to $<10^{-12}$, with a negative control confirming that
an off-diagonal sector is \emph{not} even in $\delta$
(Fig.~\ref{fig:multiplet}(b)).}
\label{tab:stabilizers}
\end{table}

The distinction matters because it is easy to over-state: reflections of the
parameter space are \emph{not} symmetries of a generic sector, and only the
three stabilized families in Table~\ref{tab:stabilizers} inherit one.

\subsection{Termination law}\label{sec:termination}

In a diagonal sector every branch is even in $\delta$ and hence, assuming
analyticity in the parameters, an analytic function of $t\equiv\delta^2$. The
discriminant of the local two-branch problem,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:D}
  D=(\omega_+-\omega_-)^2,
\end{equation}
therefore depends on $\delta$ only through $t$, and an EP2 is $D=0$: two real
conditions, the familiar codimension two \cite{Bergholtz2019E63}. In $(s,t,\mu)$
this defines a one-dimensional curve. The physical $\delta$-space, however, is
the double cover $\delta=\pm\sqrt t$, defined only for $t\ge0$. Two consequences
follow without knowing whether an EP exists:
\begin{enumerate}
\item exceptional lines occur in mirror pairs, exchanged by $E$;
\item where the $(s,t,\mu)$ curve crosses $t=0$ transversally into $t<0$, the
real locus has no continuation. Parametrizing by arclength $\tau$ with
$t\approx c\tau$ gives $\delta=\pm\sqrt{c\tau}$: the two mirror branches meet at
$\delta=0$ and \emph{stop}, approaching the equal-spin surface quadratically
rather than crossing it as one smooth line.
\end{enumerate}

This is the mechanism by which the equal-spin symmetry organizes exceptional
topology in this system --- not by protecting a degeneracy, that channel being
closed by Corollary~\ref{cor:nogo}, but by constraining the unfolding. It is the
gravitational counterpart of the symmetry-constrained exceptional structures
catalogued in non-Hermitian lattice models
\cite{Zhangetal2022E66,Mandal2021E65}, with the important difference that there
symmetry \emph{lowers} the codimension of higher-order points, whereas here it
acts on the reality structure of the unfolding parameter. The prediction is
falsifiable and was recorded before the numerical search; it remains untested,
because no exceptional line was found to exhibit it.

%=========================================================================
\section{Numerical methods and diagnostics}\label{sec:methods}
%=========================================================================

\subsection{Solvers}

Four solvers are used, in two independent families. Solver~A is Leaver's
continued fraction \cite{Leaver1985D51,LeaverD52} applied to the
Gaussian-reduced Frobenius recurrence, whose width is $13$ for generic two-spin
parameters and $9$ in the static case. Solver~B uses the raw recurrence with a
Hill determinant and Wynn acceleration \cite{Hatsuda2021D49}; it shares A's
recurrence and is \emph{not} independent of it. Solver~C is an exterior
complex-scaled Chebyshev collocation, and Solver~D a multidomain near-horizon
spectral method; both are recurrence-free, and C's independence is enforced
structurally by a test that fails if any recurrence routine is referenced. An
arbitrary-precision variant of the whole chain is available via \texttt{mpmath}.
Related matrix and spectral approaches are surveyed in
\cite{Choetal2011D57,Lin2016D58,Linetal2017D59,Matyjasek2017D60,Fortuna2020D62},
and open implementations for Kerr in \cite{Stein2019D61}.

Any claim requires agreement between the two families; two wrappers around one
discretization are not independent evidence. The atlas domain reaches
$r_-=0.2287$, beyond the previously validated $r_-\le0.19$; Solvers~A and~C
agree to a maximum of $2.06\times10^{-9}$ on nine spanning points including the
domain corners, which is the evidence supporting the extension.

\subsection{Why $|dF/d\omega|$ cannot bound anything}\label{sec:dfdw}

A spectral condition $F(\omega)$ is defined only up to a nonvanishing analytic
factor: Leaver's continued fraction may be rescaled, or inverted at a different
depth, without changing its zero set. Consequently $|dF/d\omega|$ at a root has
no invariant meaning and can be made arbitrarily small by rescaling; any
exclusion built on it bounds nothing. Figure~\ref{fig:detector}(a) exhibits the
failure directly: two spectral conditions with identical zeros whose
$|dF/d\omega|$ differ by more than $10^5$, while the invariant diagnostic below
agrees to $2\%$.

\subsection{A rescaling-invariant diagnostic}

Near a simple root $\omega_1$ of $F=c\,(\omega-\omega_1)(\omega-\omega_2)g$ with
$g$ analytic and nonvanishing, the Taylor coefficients about $\omega_1$ obey
$a_1=c(\omega_1-\omega_2)g$ and $a_2=cg+\mathcal{O}(\omega_1-\omega_2)$, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sep}
  \left|\frac{a_1}{a_2}\right|\longrightarrow|\omega_1-\omega_2| ,
\end{equation}
with $c$ and $g$ cancelling. The estimator \eqref{eq:sep} is invariant under
rescaling of $F$, vanishes exactly at an EP2, and --- unlike a pairwise gap
between tracked branches --- detects a partner root that was never computed. The
coefficients come from a Cauchy integral on a circle, which also yields the
argument-principle zero count for free; root recovery from contour moments
follows \cite{KravanjaVanBarel2000}.

\subsection{Verification gate, validated on synthetic systems}

A detector that has never been shown to fire cannot support a negative result.
The machinery is therefore validated against closed-form problems whose
exceptional structure is known --- $\lambda^2-t$ (EP2), $\lambda^3-t$ (EP3),
$\lambda^2-(t^2+g^2)$ (avoided crossing), Jordan blocks, and block-diagonal
coincidences --- including \emph{negative controls}, in which the detector is
required not to fire. Figure~\ref{fig:detector} shows three of these checks.
Puiseux expansions about a defective point and their numerical construction
follow the treatment of \cite{Nennig2019E67}.

A candidate is accepted only if it satisfies all of: separation $\to0$ under
refinement; argument-principle count $2$; both roots located without a starting
guess; monodromy transposing the branches on one loop and restoring them on two;
$t^{1/2}$ splitting preferred over $t^1$; stability under refinement of
resolution, depth and precision; and confirmation by a recurrence-free solver
inside its validated domain.

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig5_detector_validation.pdf}
  \caption{Calibration of the diagnostics on systems with known answers.
  (a) The estimator \eqref{eq:sep} recovers the true root separation over three
  decades and is unchanged when the spectral condition is multiplied by
  $10^7e^{3z}$; the same rescaling moves $|dF/d\omega|$ by seven orders of
  magnitude, which is why it cannot bound anything (Sec.~\ref{sec:dfdw}).
  (b) Puiseux exponent: $t^{1/2}$ at an EP2, $t^1$ at an ordinary crossing, and
  saturation at a nonzero constant for an avoided crossing.
  (c) Monodromy: transporting the two roots around a small loop in parameter
  space exchanges them at an EP2 (the phase does not return), while for an
  avoided crossing each root returns to itself.}
  \label{fig:detector}
\end{figure*}

%=========================================================================
\section{Branch atlas}\label{sec:atlas}
%=========================================================================

Branches are identified by continuation history, never by sorting frequencies:
at an avoided crossing two branches exchange order in $\Rem\,\omega$ while
remaining distinct modes, and sort-based labelling silently swaps them. Each
step is seeded by a quadratic extrapolation of the previous points and accepted
only if the corrected root agrees with the prediction to within a tolerance
drawn from the branch's \emph{own} history of predictor misses. A tolerance
proportional to $|\omega|$ is a constant, not an identity test; using one
admitted a branch jump in which $\Imm\,\omega$ reversed, and the contaminated
point became --- until it was caught --- the tightest reported candidate.

The atlas contains $50\,558$ points across seven independent sectors,
$(0,0)$, $(1,1)$, $(-1,-1)$, $(1,0)$, $(2,0)$, $(2,1)$ and $(2,2)$, with
$\ell\in\{\ell_{\min},\ell_{\min}+2,\ell_{\min}+4\}$ and $N=0,\dots,3$, over
$s\le0.42$, $|\delta|\le0.20$, $\mu\le1.8$, $r_-\le0.2287$ and extremality
$M-(|a|+|b|)^2\ge0.294$. The maximum continued-fraction residual is
$3.6\times10^{-9}$; $118$ predictor-miss and $33$ non-convergence events are
recorded rather than filled in. Table~\ref{tab:census} summarizes the census.

\centering

\toprule

\midrule

angular branches per sector & $3$ \\

Two independent symmetry predictions are recovered from the atlas as an
end-to-end consistency check: the branch gaps at $\pm\delta$ in diagonal sectors
agree to $\sim10^{-12}$, and sectors $(1,1)$ and $(2,0)$, which share $m=2$,
agree at $\delta=0$ to $9\times10^{-12}$. Neither was imposed; both are
consequences of Secs.~\ref{sec:nogo} and~\ref{sec:group} recovered from
independently computed frequencies.

%=========================================================================
\section{Result: a bounded exclusion}\label{sec:result}
%=========================================================================

At every parameter point we compute the minimum pairwise gap between distinct
branches of the same sector; at the tightest candidates and a deterministic
random subsample we additionally compute the invariant separator \eqref{eq:sep}.
The two tiers fail in different directions --- the gap sees only branches that
were computed, while \eqref{eq:sep} sees any nearby zero --- and using both is
what makes the result trustworthy, as Sec.~\ref{sec:collapse} illustrates.
Over the whole domain,
\begin{align}\label{eq:bounds}
  \min|\omega_i-\omega_j| &= 0.5116, &
  \min|a_1/a_2| &= 0.3107, \nonumber\\
  \min|D| &= 0.2618, &
  \kappa_{\max} &= 8.73\times10^{3},
\end{align}
against $\kappa=18.3$ at an ordinary control mode. An EP2 requires the first
three to vanish simultaneously and $\kappa$ to diverge. None approaches zero:
the minimum gap is $\approx0.51$ where $|\omega|\approx2$--$4$, a relative
separation of order $15\%$. Figure~\ref{fig:bounds} shows the distributions
behind \eqref{eq:bounds}, and Fig.~\ref{fig:gaplandscape} the gap landscape
across all seven sectors.

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig4_bounds.pdf}
  \caption{The bounds \eqref{eq:bounds}. (a) Distribution of the pairwise branch
  gap over the atlas; (b) the rescaling-invariant root separation
  \eqref{eq:sep}, which also detects partner roots absent from the atlas;
  (c) the minimum discriminant per branch pair from the effective models of
  Sec.~\ref{sec:consequences}. Red lines mark the minima. An exceptional point
  requires all three to reach zero simultaneously.}
  \label{fig:bounds}
\end{figure*}

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig3_gap_landscape.pdf}
  \caption{Gap landscape across every searched sector, between the $N=2$ and
  $N=3$ overtones of the highest angular branch, on the equal-spin surface. The
  gap varies smoothly and remains of order unity everywhere; it decreases toward
  large $s$ and $\mu$ and attains its minimum at the corner of the searched
  domain, a boundary effect discussed in Sec.~\ref{sec:limits}.}
  \label{fig:gaplandscape}
\end{figure*}

The ten tightest candidates were put through the full gate. All ten are
rejected, with a single common signature: the argument principle finds two zeros
and both are located without a guess, but there is no coalescence, no monodromy
exchange around a parameter loop, and no square-root splitting. The first two
conditions are \emph{preconditions} --- they establish only that two distinct
roots sit near each other --- so the classification is \emph{avoided crossing},
not ``unresolved''. This is the behaviour familiar from eigenvalue repulsion in
Kerr--Newman \cite{Diasetal2021B19,Davey2023B21}, here without the accompanying
exceptional points.

\subsection{Branch-label collapse, and why two tiers are necessary}
\label{sec:collapse}

Four point-pairs with gaps at machine precision were identified as
\emph{branch-label collapses}, in which continuation lost one of two labelled
branches and both labels came to designate the same mode. Their invariant
separation exceeds their apparent gap by eleven orders of magnitude, and the
argument principle finds exactly one zero inside a contour that the gap would
have suggested contains two. They are excluded and counted.

This is not a footnote. In an earlier build of the atlas the same defect
affected two hundred parameter points, and the tier-1 minimum read
$4.3\times10^{-15}$ --- a spectacular false positive that a single-diagnostic
search would have reported as a coalescence. It was caught only because the two
tiers disagreed in a way that no genuine EP can produce: a true coalescence
makes \emph{both} small, while a lost label makes the gap small and leaves the
separation of order unity.

%=========================================================================
\section{Effective model, pseudospectrum and ringdown}\label{sec:consequences}
%=========================================================================

\paragraph*{Effective model.} Two interacting branches are captured locally by a
$2\times2$ non-Hermitian generator. Its individual entries are not observable ---
any similarity transformation changes them --- but the two symmetric functions
are: the trace $T=\omega_++\omega_-$ and the discriminant $D$ of \eqref{eq:D}.
Fitting $D$ as a polynomial in $(s,t=\delta^2,\mu)$ and scoring on held-out
points gives a relative out-of-sample error of $1.7\times10^{-5}$ in the
diagonal sector $(1,1)$ but $1.4\times10^{-1}$ in the off-diagonal sector
$(2,0)$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:pseudo}(c)). The four-order-of-magnitude gap is an
independent confirmation of the $\delta$-parity classification of
Sec.~\ref{sec:group}: only diagonal sectors are analytic in $\delta^2$, so only
there is the fit in $t$ the correct model.

\paragraph*{Pseudospectrum.} Quasinormal spectra of black holes are notoriously
sensitive to perturbations of the operator
\cite{Nollert1996C33,Jaramillo2020C36,Jaramillo2021C37,Destounisetal2021C38,%
Cheungetal2021C39,Destounis2023C42,Shenetal2025C44}, and the appropriate
diagnostic is the pseudospectrum, whose interpretation depends on the norm
chosen \cite{TrefethenE72,GasperinC40}. We therefore state ours explicitly. The
operator is Solver~C's exterior-complex-scaled Chebyshev collocation matrix with
$\Lambda(\omega)$ recomputed at every $\omega$; the norm is the matrix $2$-norm
on collocation coefficients; and the eigenvalue condition number at a simple
root is
\begin{equation}
  \kappa=\frac{\|u\|\,\|v\|}{|v^\dagger T'(\omega_*)u|},
\end{equation}
with $u,v$ the right and left null vectors. This is a \emph{discretization}
norm, not a continuum energy norm, and no continuum pseudospectral claim is made
here. At the strongest interaction $\kappa=8.73\times10^3$ against $18.3$ at an
ordinary mode --- elevated by a factor $476$, as expected at a genuine avoided
crossing, but finite. Figure~\ref{fig:pseudo}(a,b) shows the corresponding
$\sigma_{\min}$ landscapes: a single clean basin at an ordinary mode, and a
deeper, elongated basin at the strongest interaction, with no sign of the
coalescing pair of minima that an approaching EP would produce.

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig7_pseudospectrum.pdf}
  \caption{Conditioning and the effective model. (a,b) Normalized smallest
  singular value of the complex-scaled collocation operator in the complex
  frequency plane, at an ordinary control mode and at the strongest interaction.
  The basin deepens and elongates but does not split into two coalescing minima.
  (c) Out-of-sample skill of the discriminant model fitted in $t=\delta^2$:
  diagonal sectors are predicted four orders of magnitude better than
  off-diagonal ones, independently confirming the $\delta$-parity of
  Sec.~\ref{sec:group}.}
  \label{fig:pseudo}
\end{figure*}

\paragraph*{Ringdown.} For a $2\times2$ generator the propagator is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{eq:propagator}
  e^{-iHt}=e^{-i\bar\omega t}\Big[\cos(\Delta t)\,\mathbb{1}
  -i\frac{\sin(\Delta t)}{\Delta}\,(H-\bar\omega\mathbb{1})\Big],
\end{equation}
with $\bar\omega=T/2$ and $\Delta=\sqrt D/2$, tending to the secular
$(A+Bt)e^{-i\bar\omega t}$ form as $D\to0$ --- the double-pole response
characteristic of an EP \cite{PanossoMacedoetal2025B30,Nakamoto2026A17}.

A tempting test is to compare the beat time
$t_{\rm beat}=2\pi/|\Rem(\omega_+-\omega_-)|$ with the damping time
$\tau=1/|\Imm\,\bar\omega|$ and call the pair EP-like whenever
$t_{\rm beat}\gg\tau$, on the grounds that the two modes then decay before they
can be resolved. \emph{That criterion is insufficient}, and this system shows
why. At the strongest interactions $t_{\rm beat}/\tau$ reaches
$1.4\times10^{4}$, yet nothing EP-like occurs: those branches split almost
entirely in $\Imm\,\omega$ (by $0.53$) rather than $\Rem\,\omega$ (by
$8\times10^{-4}$ to $0.07$), as Fig.~\ref{fig:time}(c) makes plain. They have
nearly equal oscillation frequencies but very different decay rates, so one
companion simply dies first. Secular growth requires coalescence in the
\emph{full complex} frequency, not near-degeneracy of the real parts alone.
Consistently, the EP template beats a single damped exponential by only a factor
$2.4$ in relative residual while using twice as many free amplitudes
(Fig.~\ref{fig:time}(a,b)). We find no exceptional phenomenology in the
ringdown, and note that the distinction matters for searches that use
near-degeneracy of $\Rem\,\omega$ as a proxy
\cite{Motohashi2024B24,Kubota2025B27}.

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig8_time_domain.pdf}
  \caption{Time-domain response at the strongest interaction. (a) The two-mode
  signal against the EP template $(A+Bt)e^{-i\bar\omega t}$ and a single damped
  exponential; (b) their relative residuals --- the EP template improves on a
  single mode by only a factor $2.4$ while carrying twice the free amplitudes.
  (c) The splitting of the six tightest pairs lies far above the diagonal: it is
  almost entirely in the damping rate, not the oscillation frequency, which is
  why a large $t_{\rm beat}/\tau$ does not indicate proximity to an EP.}
  \label{fig:time}
\end{figure*}

%=========================================================================
\section{The quasiresonant limit}\label{sec:quasiresonant}
%=========================================================================

Massive branches migrate toward the threshold $\omega^2=\mu^2$ as $\mu$ grows,
producing arbitrarily long-lived quasiresonances
\cite{Ponglertsakul2020A12,Lietal2023A15,Huang2025A16}. Tracking eleven branches
across six sectors with an adaptive step, the damping falls by $8.6$ orders of
magnitude along a single continuous branch, from $0.357$ at $\mu=0$ to
$8.65\times10^{-10}$ at $\mu=2.968$, with $\Rem\,\omega\to\mu$
(Fig.~\ref{fig:quasi}(a,b)). This is a branch point in $\mu$, not a coalescence:
the neighbouring overtone remains at $-\Imm\,\omega\sim0.1$ throughout, so the
branches separate rather than merge.

The same regime resolves a question about solver behaviour that turns out to be
physics rather than numerics. Exterior complex scaling requires a contour angle
satisfying $\tan\theta>-\Imm\,\Omega/\Rem\,\Omega$ so that the outgoing solution
decays along the rotated contour. As $\Rem\,\Omega\to0$ the outgoing wave ceases
to oscillate and becomes a pure growing exponential, so $\theta_{\min}\to90^\circ$
and \emph{no admissible contour exists} (Fig.~\ref{fig:quasi}(c)). We measure
$\theta_{\min}=89.92^\circ$ and $89.81^\circ$ at points where the
recurrence-free solvers fail, against $4.4^\circ$ at an ordinary near-extremal
point where they succeed. This is a formulation limit, not a convergence
failure: no increase in resolution, precision or domain decomposition can remove
it, which is precisely why a multidomain refinement of the near-horizon region
did not help.

It follows that the difficulty in this parameter range is controlled by $\mu$
and \emph{not} by proximity to extremality. Ordinary modes continue smoothly to
extremality $M-(|a|+|b|)^2=0.0103$ with residuals $\sim10^{-13}$ over $37$
consecutive steps. Attributing such failures to near-extremality --- as is
natural given the extensive literature on nearly extremal spectra
\cite{Yangetal2012B18,Cavalcante2024B23} --- would misdiagnose the mechanism
here. The principled tool for this regime is a hyperboloidal formulation, which
regularizes the outgoing behaviour geometrically rather than by rotation
\cite{Jaramillo2020C36,PanossoMacedoetal2025B30}.

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig6_quasiresonance.pdf}
  \caption{The quasiresonant limit. (a) Damping along branches followed by
  adaptive continuation in $\mu$; it falls by $8.6$ orders of magnitude. The
  walks terminate where double precision can no longer resolve the mode, so the
  minima are lower bounds on how far each branch was followed, not infima.
  (b) The approach to the threshold, $\Rem\,\omega\to\mu$. (c) The minimum
  admissible exterior-complex-scaling angle: as $\Rem\,\Omega\to0$ it reaches
  $90^\circ$ and the method has no admissible contour, independently of
  resolution or precision.}
  \label{fig:quasi}
\end{figure*}

%=========================================================================
\section{Limitations}\label{sec:limits}
%=========================================================================

The minimum gap is attained on the boundary of the searched box ($s=0.42$,
$\delta=-0.20$, $\mu=1.8$), as Fig.~\ref{fig:gaplandscape} shows. A targeted
probe beyond the box finds the gap continuing to fall to $0.472$ at $s=0.45$ but
\emph{rising} again at $\mu=3.0$ and $3.6$ (to $0.70$--$1.12$), so the trend
does not extrapolate to zero; nevertheless no claim is made for $s>0.45$ or
$\mu>1.8$. Overtones $N>3$ and higher $\ell$ were not searched, and the
behaviour of highly damped overtones is known to be delicate
\cite{Nollert1996C33,Miyachi2025C45}.

The quasiresonant regime is not searched for exceptional points. There the
recurrence-free solvers are inapplicable by formulation
(Sec.~\ref{sec:quasiresonant}), so no independent confirmation is available and
the evidentiary standard we impose cannot be met. This is the one region of the
studied sectors in which an exceptional point could still be hiding.

Certification was attempted and is deliberately limited. Using interval and ball
arithmetic \cite{MooreE73,TuckerE74,Breiding2020E69,Duff2024E70} we obtain a
Krawczyk existence/uniqueness certificate for finite-dimensional systems and an
Arb enclosure of the angular eigenvalue of the truncated Jacobi matrix,
validated by recovering the exact value $\ell(\ell+2)$ at $c^2=0$. The
\emph{radial} problem is not certified: its polynomial coefficients are obtained
by a discrete Fourier transform for which we have no rigorous aliasing bound, so
the truncation error cannot be bounded. We therefore claim no
truncated-recurrence certificate anywhere, and no continuum certificate at all.

Finally, the numerical result is a bounded exclusion over a declared domain, not
a theorem, and must not be conflated with Corollary~\ref{cor:nogo}, which is
exact and holds everywhere.

%=========================================================================
\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
%=========================================================================

Exceptional lines \emph{do} occur in the de Sitter members of this family, in
the plane spanned by scalar mass and spin and in the near-Nariai limit
\cite{Nakamoto2026A17}. Our $\Lambda=0$ result is a contrast between spacetimes,
not a contradiction: the de Sitter mechanism relies on the cosmological horizon
and the P\"oschl--Teller reduction, neither of which has an asymptotically flat
analogue, and the eigenvalue repulsions that accompany it
\cite{Daveyetal2022A13} are a de Sitter phenomenon. Nothing here is evidence
about those results.

Within the asymptotically flat doubly rotating case the structure we find is
sharply organized. The most natural route to exceptional behaviour is closed
exactly, by the same symmetry that creates the candidate degeneracies. The
surviving route --- collisions between $(\ell,N)$ branches inside a sector --- is
numerically weak: those branches repel with a gap that never falls below half a
unit, and they interact predominantly through their damping rates rather than
their frequencies, so even the strongest interaction leaves no imprint on the
ringdown. It is worth emphasizing that this is a statement about a
\emph{four}-dimensional problem in disguise: the doubly rotating background
offers two spin parameters and a mass, i.e.\ exactly the parameter count at
which codimension-two exceptional sets should be generic
\cite{Bergholtz2019E63}. Their absence is therefore informative rather than
expected.

Two methodological points may outlive the specific application. First, the
derivative of a spectral condition is not an invariant and cannot bound the
distance to an exceptional point; searches that use it should be re-examined.
Second, a small computed gap between two \emph{labels} is evidence about the
labels before it is evidence about the physics, and a search with a single
diagnostic cannot tell the two apart.

The natural next step is a hyperboloidal formulation, the only method that
remains applicable as $\Rem\,\Omega\to0$ and therefore the only way to search the
quasiresonant regime --- the sole region of the studied sectors that this work
could not cover.

\section{Reproduction and data availability}\label{app:repro}

All code, machine-readable results and reproduction scripts are available at the
project repository. The central result is regenerated by a single command from a
clean clone; the branch atlas is regenerated from a deterministic driver and
verified against a per-shard SHA-256 manifest rather than distributed. Every
figure in this paper is generated from the same JSON records that the text
quotes, so no figure can drift from the result it illustrates. Solver domains,
benchmarks, the full verification gate, the certification scope and a record of
failed approaches are given in the Supplemental Material.
